Cantor Point

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Drag the corners of a triangle and watch three lines meet at one spot, right in the middle of a circle.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Press the buttons to show or hide each part of the picture.
Look for the math

Three lines drawn from the sides of a triangle towards its corners always meet at one point. That point turns out to be the centre of a circle that runs through the middles of the sides. Drag a corner and watch: the meeting point moves, but the three lines still agree.

The triangle outside the circle

Every triangle has a circumcircle through its three corners. A tangent to that circle at A is a straight line that just touches it there. The tangents at A, B and C form a new triangle around the circle: the tangential triangle. Its side opposite the tangents at B and C is the tangent at A.

Three perpendicular lines

Let mA be the midpoint of BC. From mA, draw the line that crosses the tangent at A at a right angle; do the same at B and C. These are Cantor's lines. The page claims they are always concurrent, and the logic test checks this on hundreds of triangles: they do meet, every time.

Why they all meet at one point

Put the origin at the circle's centre O and write the corners as z_A, z_B, z_C. Then m_A = (z_B + z_C)/2 and the centre of the nine-point circle is N = (z_A + z_B + z_C)/2. Subtract: N - m_A = z_A/2, so the line from mA to N is parallel to the radius OA and therefore perpendicular to the tangent at A. The same calculation works at B and C, so all three lines pass through N.

N = (A + B + C - O)/2  and  radius of nine-point circle = radius of circumcircle / 2.

More sides, same point

The page's remark goes further. For any shape inscribed in a circle, take one vertex p and the centroid g of all the other vertices. The line through g perpendicular to the tangent at p always passes through one common point, (sum of all vertices - O)/(n - 1). For a triangle, n = 3 and that point is the nine-point centre N again; the logic test checks this for shapes with 3 to 7 sides.

Try dragging a corner until its angle is a right angle: the two opposite tangents become parallel, but the three Cantor lines still meet at N.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
